evidence: src/infrastructure/in-memory.ts: InMemoryProductRepository implements ProductRepository, InMemoryOrderRepository implements OrderRepository, SystemClock implements Clock, UuidGenerator implements IdGenerator: these implement the domain interfaces.
src/infrastructure/seed.ts: seedCatalogue(products: ProductRepository) loads data only through products.save(new Product(...)), so it goes through the abstraction.

src/infrastructure/server.ts: builds InMemory* repositories, calls seedCatalogue, and passes OrderService and InventoryService into createApp, acting purely as the setup code that wires the app together.

src/infrastructure/http.ts: route handlers hand work to services.orders.* and services.inventory.*, and state validation calls the domain's isOrderState and ORDER_STATES, so the rule is not redefined here.

src/infrastructure/http.ts: the /orders/:id/transitions handler repeats parseStateQuery's check `typeof state !== "string" || !isOrderState(state)` and its error message. This is minor duplication within one file, and both copies use the single domain rule.
parsedVerdict.reasoning: The module is the infrastructure adapter layer, and its four files cover parts of that one concern. http.ts translates between HTTP and the application services (createApp, AppServices, toErrorResponse) and hands all business work to OrderService and InventoryService. in-memory.ts implements the domain interfaces (ProductRepository, OrderRepository, Clock, IdGenerator). seed.ts loads the starter catalogue through the ProductRepository interface and the domain Product constructor. server.ts builds the app and wires everything together using only each file's public API. Nothing in the module bypasses its own abstractions: seed.ts calls ProductRepository.save rather than touching the Map, and server.ts uses createApp instead of building express routes itself. The order-state rule lives in the domain (isOrderState, ORDER_STATES), and http.ts calls it rather than restating it. One small issue: the /orders/:id/transitions handler repeats the type check and error message that parseStateQuery already contains, instead of sharing one helper. Both copies rely on the same domain rule, so this is minor duplication within one file, not a split invariant. Another: SystemClock and UuidGenerator sit in a file named in-memory.ts, which is a naming mismatch rather than a cohesion break.
